headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Emergency Contraception
headings.content: **Emergency contraception (EC)** refers to safe medical methods used by women to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sexual intercourse, contraceptive failure, or sexual assault. It acts as a crucial backup plan, not a primary form of family planning. These methods are designed to intercept the fertilization process before implantation occurs in the uterine lining. They do not disrupt an established pregnancy or act as an abortifacient. Understanding this distinction is vital for nurses when educating clients and managing moral or cultural misconceptions in healthcare settings.

headings.title: Indications and Timing for Emergency Contraceptive Use
headings.content:
Timing is the single most critical factor determining the success of emergency contraception. The sooner a method is used after unprotected intercourse, the higher its effectiveness. Common indications include forgotten oral contraceptive pills, broken condoms, displaced diaphragms, missed injection windows, or sexual assault.

- **Unprotected Intercourse**: Any act of sexual intercourse without barrier or hormonal protection.
- **Contraceptive Mishap**: Slipping, breaking, or tearing of a condom during use.
- **Calculation Error**: Misjudging the fertile window during natural family planning methods.
- **Coercion**: Instances of sexual assault where regular contraception was absent.

headings.title: Mechanism of Action: How Emergency Contraception Works
headings.content: Most emergency contraceptive pills work primarily by delaying or preventing ovulation. If a woman has already ovulated before taking the medication, hormonal pills will not stop fertilization or implantation. This explains why timing matters so much in the menstrual cycle. The copper intrauterine device works differently by creating a spermicidal local inflammatory environment that prevents fertilization and blocks implantation entirely.

headings.title: Types of Emergency Contraceptive Pills
headings.content:
Several pharmacological options exist for emergency hormonal contraception, varying by active ingredient and time limits:

- **Levonorgestrel (LNG)**: Available widely over-the-counter as brands like Postinor-2. Most effective when taken within 72 hours (3 days), though some effect remains up to 120 hours.
- **Ulipristal Acetate (UPA)**: A selective progesterone receptor modulator requiring a prescription. It remains effective up to 120 hours (5 days) and maintains higher efficacy closer to the time of ovulation compared to levonorgestrel.

headings.title: The Copper Intrauterine Device as Emergency Contraception
headings.content: The **copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD)** is the most effective form of emergency contraception available. It can be inserted by a trained provider up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected intercourse. Beyond serving as an emergency method, it provides ongoing, highly effective contraception for years if the client desires. It is an excellent choice for women wanting long-term reversible birth control, though it requires a clinical procedure for insertion.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment, Counseling, and Patient History
headings.content: Before providing emergency contraception, nurses must conduct a focused clinical assessment. The nurse should ask about the exact timing of the unprotected intercourse, the date of the last normal menstrual period to rule out an existing pregnancy, and any history of severe allergies or medical conditions. Confidentiality and a non-judgmental attitude are paramount, especially when caring for adolescents or survivors of sexual violence.

headings.title: Side Effects, Contraindications, and Follow-up Care
headings.content: Emergency contraceptive pills are generally safe, but clients may experience temporary side effects like nausea, fatigue, headache, and irregular spotting or a delayed next period. If a client vomits within two hours of taking a hormonal pill, the dose may need to be repeated. Follow-up care includes advising the client to take a pregnancy test if their period is delayed by more than a week.

headings.title: Addressing Myths, Barriers, and the Nurse's Role in Nigeria
headings.content: In Nigeria, cultural stigma, religious beliefs, and misinformation often hinder access to emergency contraception. Many young people mistakenly believe emergency contraceptives cause permanent infertility or are equivalent to criminal abortion. Nurses play a frontline role in community education, dispelling these myths, providing youth-friendly services, and ensuring clients can access safe reproductive health commodities without fear or judgment.
